mcqs.question: What is the main readability benefit of a CTE over nesting the same logic as subqueries?
options: It lets you name each intermediate step and reference it, avoiding several levels of nested parentheses
It automatically makes the query run faster than any subquery version
It removes the need to write a FROM clause
It allows the query to skip validation of column names
mcqs.explanation: CTEs turn nested subqueries into a linear, named sequence of steps that reads top to bottom. They don't guarantee a speed improvement (that depends on materialization behavior), and they don't change FROM clause or validation requirements.

mcqs.question: In a recursive CTE, what does the anchor member do?
options: It produces a running count of how many recursive iterations have occurred
It validates that the recursive member's syntax is correct before execution
It produces the starting set of rows that the recursive member then builds on
It defines the maximum recursion depth allowed
mcqs.explanation: The anchor member is a normal, non-recursive query that seeds the starting rows; the recursive member then repeatedly extends from there. It doesn't track iteration counts, validate syntax, or set a depth cap on its own.

mcqs.question: A recursive CTE walking an org chart runs forever until the engine times out. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The anchor member returned zero rows
The data contains a cycle (or the recursive member never restricts to unvisited rows), so no pass ever produces zero new rows
The CTE was declared without the WITH keyword
The query is missing a GROUP BY clause
mcqs.explanation: Recursion only stops when an iteration adds zero new rows; a data cycle or a missing visited-guard means that never happens. A zero-row anchor would make the query return nothing immediately, not loop forever; the other two options are unrelated syntax issues.

mcqs.question: You need to reuse an intermediate result across three separate SQL statements in the same session, and want to add an index to it. What should you use?
options: A plain subquery repeated in each statement
A non-recursive CTE
A recursive CTE
A temporary table
mcqs.explanation: Only a temp table persists across separate statements and can be indexed — a CTE's scope is limited to the single query it's defined in. A repeated subquery would need rewriting three times and can't be indexed either.

mcqs.question: Why might a CTE-based query perform worse on an older PostgreSQL version than the equivalent rewritten as a subquery?
options: Older PostgreSQL always materialized non-recursive CTEs, blocking the optimizer from pushing outer-query filters into them
CTEs are not valid syntax on older PostgreSQL versions
PostgreSQL executes CTEs on a different, slower storage engine
Subqueries always use a different index than CTEs regardless of version
mcqs.explanation: Pre-v12 Postgres always materialized non-recursive CTEs as an optimization fence, sometimes preventing helpful filter pushdown that a plain subquery would have allowed. CTEs are valid SQL on all these versions, there's no separate storage engine, and index usage isn't automatically tied to CTE vs subquery syntax.

mcqs.question: Why should you add an explicit depth limit to a recursive CTE even if you believe the source data has no cycles?
options: Depth limits are required by the SQL standard for all recursive queries
A cycle-free hierarchy can still grow unexpectedly deep on a bad branch, and a runaway depth can return far more rows than expected or time out
Without a depth limit, the query cannot use the UNION ALL keyword
It has no real benefit; it is only a stylistic convention
mcqs.explanation: Absence of cycles doesn't bound depth — a data-entry mistake can make one branch far deeper than intended, and an uncapped recursive CTE will walk all of it. There's no SQL-standard depth requirement, no connection to UNION ALL syntax, and the safeguard has real practical value, not just style.
